claim: The N2G-JM-TSMod displays higher tension (lower FRET index) than the no-tension NoT_TSMod control when expressed in MKCs plated on FN-coated glass.
source: The N2G-JM-TSMod displays higher tension (lower FRET index) than the no-tension NoT_TSMod control (higher FRET index) when expressed in MKCs plated on FN-coated glass.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 1B-C comparing the two constructs, with quantitative data showing statistically significant differences (p<0.0001).

claim: Disruption of actin filaments with 0.5 μM latrunculin A decreases the tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod, leading to a higher FRET index.
source: Disruption of actin filaments with 0.5 μM latrunculin A (Lat A) decreases the tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod, leading to a higher FRET index.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D-E showing increased FRET index upon latrunculin A treatment compared to vehicle control (p<0.0001).

claim: Tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod is sensitive to substrate mechanics, with MKCs on compliant substrates (3 kPa PDMS) showing increased FRET compared to cells on glass.
source: Tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod is sensitive to substrate mechanics. Plating of MKCs on FN-coated compliant substrates (3 kPa PDMS) leads to increased FRET compared to MKCs plated on FN-coated glass.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements in Figure 1F-G comparing FRET indices on different substrate stiffnesses (p<0.0001).

claim: MKCs grown on glass coated with fibronectin or laminin drive higher tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod than cells grown on poly-L-lysine-coated glass.
source: Plating of MKCs on extracellular matrix that engages integrins drives high tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod. MKCs grown on glass coated with fibronectin or laminin drive a higher tension state (low FRET index) than for cells grown on glass coated with poly-L-lysine (high FRET index).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET measurements in Figure 1H-I showing statistically significant differences between substrate types (p<0.0001).

claim: MKCs lacking β1 integrin fail to drive high tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod.
source: MKCs lacking β1 integrin fail to drive high tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in Figure 1J-K comparing wild-type and β1 integrin null MKCs (p<0.0001).

claim: β1 integrin engagement with the extracellular matrix is required for high tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod.
source: Higher FRET indexes at the nuclear envelope in β1 integrin null MKCs demonstrate that β1 integrin engagement with the extracellular matrix is required for high tension on the N2G-JM-TSMod.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing relaxed tension (higher FRET) in β1 integrin null cells compared to wild-type.

claim: The FRET ratio of the N2G-JM-TSMod for interior cells in cohesive MKC colonies is significantly higher than that observed for cells at the colony periphery.
source: We find that the FRET ratio of the N2G-JM-TSMod for interior cells is significantly higher than that observed for cells at the colony periphery (Figure 2B), indicating that tension on the LINC complex is lost in interior cells that contain solely cell-cell adhesions.
evidence: Supported by quantitative FRET measurements comparing periphery and interior cells in Figure 2B (p=0.0005).

claim: Tension on the LINC complex is lost in interior cells that contain solely cell-cell adhesions.
source: We find that the FRET ratio of the N2G-JM-TSMod for interior cells is significantly higher than that observed for cells at the colony periphery (Figure 2B), indicating that tension on the LINC complex is lost in interior cells that contain solely cell-cell adhesions.
evidence: Inferred from the FRET measurements showing higher FRET (lower tension) in interior cells that lack focal adhesions.

claim: Cells at the colony periphery display a strong bias of conformationally sensitive lamin A/C fluorescence at the apical nuclear surface compared to the basal surface.
source: In cells at the colony periphery, we observe a strong bias of fluorescence at the apical nuclear surface compared to the basal surface (Figure 2D), indicating that tension on the lamin network is high on the basal surface in cells at the periphery of colonies.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis of lamin A/C antibody staining in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Tension on the lamin network is high on the basal surface in cells at the periphery of colonies.
source: In cells at the colony periphery, we observe a strong bias of fluorescence at the apical nuclear surface compared to the basal surface (Figure 2D), indicating that tension on the lamin network is high on the basal surface in cells at the periphery of colonies.
evidence: Inferred from the conformationally sensitive antibody staining pattern showing reduced signal on the basal surface where tension is high.

claim: Cells in the colony interior display far more uniform conformationally sensitive lamin A/C staining compared to periphery cells.
source: By contrast, cells in the colony interior display far more uniform conformationally sensitive lamin A/C staining (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis in Figure 2D-E showing histogram distribution of basal to apical intensity ratios.

claim: MKCs at the colony interior express more Sprr1b mRNA 24 and 48 hr after induction of differentiation compared to cells at the colony periphery.
source: We find that MKCs at the colony interior express more Sprr1b and Ivl (involucrin) mRNA 24 and 48 hr after induction of differentiation compared to cells at the colony periphery (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 2F-G showing statistically significant differences (p<0.05, p<0.01).

claim: MKCs at the colony interior express more Ivl (involucrin) mRNA 24 and 48 hr after induction of differentiation compared to cells at the colony periphery.
source: We find that MKCs at the colony interior express more Sprr1b and Ivl (involucrin) mRNA 24 and 48 hr after induction of differentiation compared to cells at the colony periphery (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing statistically significant differences.

claim: SUN1 and SUN2 are expressed at the nuclear envelope in all cellular layers of the E15.5 developing epidermis.
source: Similar to our prior analysis of postnatal mouse skin (Stewart et al., 2015), SUN1 and SUN2 are expressed at the nuclear envelope in all cellular layers of the E15.5 developing epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SUN1 and SUN2 proteins are absent in the skin of Sun dKO mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that SUN1 and SUN2 proteins were absent in the skin of Sun dKO compared to wild-type (WT mice that express both SUN proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B (now labeled as 1C in the figure supplement).

claim: Histological analysis of E15.5 skin tissue revealed a thickening of the epidermis in the Sun dKO mouse compared to WT littermates.
source: Histological analysis of E15.5 skin tissue revealed a thickening of the epidermis in the Sun dKO mouse compared to WT littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin staining in Figure 3A.

claim: Sun dKO mice show expansion of keratin 10 (K10) and K1 in the spinous layer.
source: Immunostaining of skin sections of WT and Sun dKO mice with antibodies against proteins expressed in differentiated keratinocytes revealed an expansion of keratin 10 (K10) and K1 in the spinous layer, involucrin in the spinous and granular layers, and fillagrin in the granular and cornified layers (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and quantitation in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B showing statistically significant increases (p<0.01).

claim: Sun dKO mice show expansion of involucrin in the spinous and granular layers.
source: Immunostaining of skin sections of WT and Sun dKO mice with antibodies against proteins expressed in differentiated keratinocytes revealed an expansion of keratin 10 (K10) and K1 in the spinous layer, involucrin in the spinous and granular layers, and fillagrin in the granular and cornified layers (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and quantitation in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-D showing statistically significant increases (p<0.01).

claim: Sun dKO mice show expansion of filaggrin in the granular and cornified layers.
source: Immunostaining of skin sections of WT and Sun dKO mice with antibodies against proteins expressed in differentiated keratinocytes revealed an expansion of keratin 10 (K10) and K1 in the spinous layer, involucrin in the spinous and granular layers, and fillagrin in the granular and cornified layers (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and quantitation in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F showing statistically significant increases (p<0.01).

claim: The total number of EdU-positive cells is similar between WT and Sun dKO epidermis.
source: Immunostaining skin sections with K10 antibodies and staining for EdU incorporation revealed that the total number of EdU-positive cells was similar between WT and Sun dKO epidermis, indicating that proliferation was not altered in the absence of LINC complexes in skin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU pulse-chase experiment and quantitation in Figure 3E showing no significant difference.

claim: Proliferation is not altered in the absence of LINC complexes in skin.
source: Immunostaining skin sections with K10 antibodies and staining for EdU incorporation revealed that the total number of EdU-positive cells was similar between WT and Sun dKO epidermis, indicating that proliferation was not altered in the absence of LINC complexes in skin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Inferred from the EdU incorporation data showing similar total EdU-positive cells between genotypes.

claim: 40% of EdU-positive cells had moved to the suprabasal, K10-positive layer in WT tissue 24 hours after EdU pulse.
source: However, while 40% of EdU-positive cells had moved to the suprabasal, K10-positive layer in WT tissue (Figure 3F), 60% of EdU-positive cells were observed in the differentiated layers in Sun dKO skin (Figure 3D, F), indicating an increase in keratinocyte differentiation in the absence of LINC complexes.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU pulse-chase experiment and quantitation in Figure 3F.

claim: 60% of EdU-positive cells were observed in the differentiated layers in Sun dKO skin 24 hours after EdU pulse.
source: However, while 40% of EdU-positive cells had moved to the suprabasal, K10-positive layer in WT tissue (Figure 3F), 60% of EdU-positive cells were observed in the differentiated layers in Sun dKO skin (Figure 3D, F), indicating an increase in keratinocyte differentiation in the absence of LINC complexes.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU pulse-chase experiment and quantitation in Figure 3D, F showing statistically significant difference (p<0.01).

claim: There is an increase in keratinocyte differentiation in the absence of LINC complexes.
source: However, while 40% of EdU-positive cells had moved to the suprabasal, K10-positive layer in WT tissue (Figure 3F), 60% of EdU-positive cells were observed in the differentiated layers in Sun dKO skin (Figure 3D, F), indicating an increase in keratinocyte differentiation in the absence of LINC complexes.
evidence: Inferred from the EdU pulse-chase data showing more EdU-positive cells in differentiated layers in Sun dKO mice.

claim: The basal layer-basal lamina interface in Sun1/2+/- and Sun dKO skin appears indistinguishable, displaying tight association in mice from both genotypes.
source: The basal layer-basal lamina interface in Sun1/2+/- and Sun dKO skin appeared indistinguishable, displaying tight association in mice from both genotypes (Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 3G.

claim: Hemidesmosomes are of equivalent number and size in Sun1/2+/- and Sun dKO mice.
source: Moreover, hemidesmosomes (which can be observed in electron micrographs, arrows) were of equivalent number and size (Figure 3H).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy and quantitation in Figure 3H showing no significant differences.

claim: Sun dKO mice display precocious epidermal differentiation in vivo that is uncoupled from changes in adhesion between basal keratinocytes and the basal lamina.
source: These observations suggest that Sun dKO mice display precocious epidermal differentiation in vivo that is uncoupled from changes in adhesion between basal keratinocytes and the basal lamina.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of differentiation data and normal hemidesmosome structure/number.

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed striking differences in the expression of genes associated with keratinocyte differentiation between WT and Sun dKO MKCs in both low and high calcium.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed striking differences in the expression of genes associated with keratinocyte differentiation between WT and Sun dKO MKCs in both low and high calcium, including those that reside in the EDC (Figure 4A, B and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and supplementary files.

claim: Numerous members of the gene family in the SPRR region of the EDC were de-repressed in Sun dKO MKCs grown in the low calcium condition.
source: For example, numerous members of the gene family in the SPRR region of the EDC (Figure 4A) were de-repressed in Sun dKO MKCs grown in the low calcium condition (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq data in Figure 4C showing elevated FPKM values for SPRR genes in Sun dKO cells.

claim: Sun dKO MKCs display precocious expression of Sprr1b when cultured in low calcium media.
source: Not only do we observe precocious expression of genes such as Sprr1b in Sun dKO MKCs cultured in low calcium media, but we also observe much higher expression in the presence of calcium in Sun dKO MKCs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Validated by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 4D showing statistically significant increases (p<0.05).

claim: Sun dKO MKCs display much higher expression of Sprr1b in the presence of calcium compared to WT MKCs.
source: Not only do we observe precocious expression of genes such as Sprr1b in Sun dKO MKCs cultured in low calcium media, but we also observe much higher expression in the presence of calcium in Sun dKO MKCs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Validated by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 4D showing statistically significant increases (p<0.05).

claim: Sun dKO MKC colonies express Sprr1b mRNAs in MKCs residing in both the interior and periphery.
source: While we demonstrated that WT MKCs biased expression of differentiation markers such as Sprr1b and Ivl at the colony interior over the colony periphery (Figure 2F, G) in agreement with repressive signals from integrin engagement in cells at the colony periphery, Sun dKO MKC colonies instead expressed Sprr1b mRNAs in MKCs residing in both the interior and periphery (Figure 4E), despite still having focal adhesions in peripheral cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA FISH in Figure 4E showing Sprr1b expression throughout Sun dKO colonies.

claim: Expression of differentiation markers is both elevated at the colony periphery and is random with respect to colony position in the absence of LINC complexes.
source: As a consequence, expression of differentiation markers is both elevated at the colony periphery and is random with respect to colony position in the absence of LINC complexes (Figure 4H, Figure 4G).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA FISH quantitation in Figure 4G-H showing no significant bias in Sprr1b location in Sun dKO colonies.

claim: β1 integrin null MKCs display precocious expression of Sprr1b, Involucrin (Ivl), and S100a14 epidermal differentiation genes.
source: β1 integrin null MKCs displayed precocious expression of all three of these epidermal differentiation genes (Figure 4I), mirroring our observations in Sun dKO MKCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 4I showing statistically significant increases (p<0.05).

claim: LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation genes when integrins are actively engaged.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation genes when integrins are actively engaged.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of data showing precocious differentiation in Sun dKO cells and loss of position-dependent differentiation despite intact focal adhesions.

claim: Sun dKO MKCs displayed almost twice as many ATAC-seq peaks within the EDC region (34 peaks) relative to WT MKCs (19 peaks).
source: It is therefore striking that Sun dKO MKCs displayed almost twice as many ATAC-seq peaks within the EDC region (34 peaks) relative to WT MKCs (19 peaks) (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: In Sun dKO MKCs there are 18 additional ATAC-seq peaks, 16 maintained peaks, and a loss of just 3 peaks in the EDC compared to WT MKCs.
source: Specifically, in Sun dKO MKCs we observed 18 additional peaks, 16 maintained peaks, and a loss of just 3 peaks compared to WT MKCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SPRR region displays the most striking change in ATAC-seq peaks, gaining five novel peaks upon loss of SUN proteins.
source: This net gain of peaks is observed throughout all regions of the EDC, with the SPRR region displaying the most striking change, gaining five novel ATAC-seq peaks upon loss of SUN proteins (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The gain of ATAC-seq peaks is more pronounced in the EDC compared to chromatin regions 5′ and 3′.
source: Importantly, while there is a trend toward increased chromatin accessibility in regions flanking the EDC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) in line with a trend toward increased accessibility across the genome (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the gain of ATAC-seq peaks is more pronounced in the EDC compared to chromatin regions 5′ and 3′ (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis and quantitation in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The changes in chromatin accessibility support a model in which keratinocyte differentiation genes are precociously expressed in Sun dKO cells despite largely normal accessibility at genes that underlie progenitor maintenance.
source: Thus, the changes in chromatin accessibility support a model in which keratinocyte differentiation genes are precociously expressed in Sun dKO cells despite largely normal accessibility at genes that underlie progenitor maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from the ATAC-seq data showing specific changes at differentiation genes but not proliferation genes.

claim: LINC complex tension in MKCs responds specifically to β1 integrin engagement in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Here, we demonstrate that LINC complex tension in MKCs responds specifically to β1 integrin engagement in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: Supported by multiple FRET experiments showing tension dependence on β1 integrin and substrate engagement.

claim: In the absence of functional LINC complexes, basal progenitors differentiate precociously both in vitro and in vivo.
source: While β1 integrin-dependent signals normally repress the differentiation of keratinocytes, in the absence of functional LINC complexes these basal progenitors instead differentiate precociously both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental data including EdU pulse-chase, RNA FISH, RT-qPCR, and immunostaining.

claim: LINC complexes transmit forces from the β1 integrin-engaged actin network to the nuclear lamina to directly regulate the expression of epidermal differentiation genes.
source: Based on our findings, we propose a model in which LINC complexes transmit forces from the β1 integrin-engaged actin network to the nuclear lamina to directly regulate the expression of epidermal differentiation genes (Figure 6), although an indirect role for the LINC complex in an alternative signaling pathway remains possible.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of all experimental findings, with acknowledgment of alternative possibilities.

claim: Adhesion between basal keratinocytes and the basal lamina remains normal in Sun dKO animals.
source: In particular, as our electron microscopy data strongly suggest that adhesion between basal keratinocytes and the basal lamina remains normal in Sun dKO animals, we strongly favor this direct model (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 3G-H showing normal hemidesmosome structure and number.

claim: High Rho activity and actin contractility are not sufficient to drive tension on the LINC complex.
source: Interestingly, our data indicate that high Rho activity and actin contractility are not sufficient to drive tension on the LINC complex – indeed, this represents a critical point that lies at the heart of our model.
evidence: Supported by observations in colony interior cells and β1 integrin null cells that have high contractility but low LINC tension.

claim: Cells at the interior of cohesive MKC colonies display extensive stress fibers integrated at cell-cell adhesions but show low tension on the LINC complex and the nuclear lamina.
source: For instance, cells at the interior of cohesive MKC colonies also display extensive stress fibers integrated at cell-cell adhesions (Mertz et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2015), but nonetheless show low tension on the LINC complex and the nuclear lamina, as demonstrated in Figure 2A–D.
evidence: Supported by FRET and lamin A/C antibody data in Figure 2, with citations to prior work on stress fiber organization.

claim: Actomyosin contractility is not sufficient, in and of itself, to drive LINC complex tension.
source: These observations suggest that actomyosin contractility is not sufficient, in and of itself, to drive LINC complex tension.
evidence: Inferred from observations that cells with high contractility but lacking β1 integrin engagement show low LINC tension.

claim: The LINC complex is relaxed in MKCs lacking β1 integrin, which have high Rho activity, strong focal adhesions (nucleated through β6 integrin), and massive stress fibers.
source: This point is underscored by our finding that the LINC complex is relaxed in MKCs lacking β1 integrin, which have high Rho activity, strong focal adhesions (nucleated through β6 integrin), and massive stress fibers (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2012; Raghavan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by FRET data in Figure 1J-K and citations to prior work characterizing β1 integrin null cells.

claim: A skin-specific lamin-null mouse model (Lamin B1/B2/A/C triple-knockout) exhibits a thickened epidermis attributed to precocious differentiation.
source: Lastly, a skin-specific lamin-null mouse model (Lamin B1/B2/A/C triple-knockout) exhibits a thickened epidermis attributed to precocious differentiation (Jung et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: During basal stem cell differentiation, the epidermal differentiation complex (EDC) relocates away from the nuclear lamina toward the nuclear interior to be transcriptionally activated.
source: First, during basal stem cell differentiation, a large chromosomal region termed the epidermal differentiation complex (EDC), which consists of 60 consecutive genes necessary for epidermal stratification and the production of the cornified envelope, relocates away from the nuclear lamina toward the nuclear interior to be transcriptionally activated (Gdula et al., 2013; Mardaryev et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: The AP-1 transcription factor complex, itself regulated by A-type lamins, influences EDC gene expression in both proliferating and differentiating keratinocytes in vitro.
source: Further, the AP-1 transcription factor complex, itself regulated by A-type lamins, influences EDC gene expression in both proliferating and differentiating keratinocytes in vitro (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: AP-1 coordinates with EZH2 in the polycomb complex, which promotes targeting of chromatin to the nuclear lamina and regulates epidermal differentiation.
source: AP-1 also coordinates with EZH2 in the polycomb complex, which promotes targeting of chromatin to the nuclear lamina (Harr et al., 2015) and regulates epidermal differentiation (Ezhkova et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: Epidermal stem cells adhere to the underlying basal lamina through β1 integrin-based adhesions and β4 integrin-based hemidesmosomes.
source: Epidermal stem cells adhere to the underlying basal lamina through β1 integrin-based adhesions and β4 integrin-based hemidesmosomes (Raghavan et al., 2000), which maintain stem cell fate, proliferation, and inhibit differentiation (Hotchin et al., 1995; Levy et al., 2000; Rippa et al., 2013; Watt et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: β1 integrin-based adhesions and β4 integrin-based hemidesmosomes maintain stem cell fate, proliferation, and inhibit differentiation.
source: Epidermal stem cells adhere to the underlying basal lamina through β1 integrin-based adhesions and β4 integrin-based hemidesmosomes (Raghavan et al., 2000), which maintain stem cell fate, proliferation, and inhibit differentiation (Hotchin et al., 1995; Levy et al., 2000; Rippa et al., 2013; Watt et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: Upon differentiation, basal keratinocytes release their integrin-based adhesions and initiate gene expression changes to activate terminal differentiation.
source: Upon differentiation, basal keratinocytes release their integrin-based adhesions, initiate gene expression changes to activate terminal differentiation (Tsuruta et al., 2011), and move upward to enter the stratified epithelium until they are shed at the skin's surface.
evidence: Cited from prior published work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The LINC complex, composed of tail-anchored Nesprins integrated into the outer nuclear membrane and SUN proteins integrated into the inner nuclear membrane, spans the nuclear envelope to mechanically integrate the cytoplasmic cytoskeleton and the nuclear interior.
source: The LINC complex, composed of tail-anchored Nesprins integrated into the outer nuclear membrane and SUN proteins integrated into the inner nuclear membrane, spans the nuclear envelope to mechanically integrate the cytoplasmic cytoskeleton and the nuclear interior – specifically the nuclear lamina and its associated chromatin (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior published work and represents established knowledge about LINC complex structure.

claim: The mTFP-Venus TSMod has been shown previously to be sensitive to forces in the single pN range.
source: The mTFP-Venus TSMod has been shown previously to be sensitive to forces in the single pN range (Grashoff et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior published work characterizing the tension sensor module.

claim: Primary MKCs can be induced to differentiate in vitro by elevating extracellular calcium levels, leading to the formation of cohesive colonies that engage E-cadherin-based cell-cell adhesions.
source: Primary MKCs can be induced to differentiate in vitro by elevating extracellular calcium levels, leading to the formation of cohesive colonies that engage E-cadherin-based cell-cell adhesions and subsequently differentiate as assessed by upregulation of markers expressed in epidermal suprabasal layers in vivo (Mertz et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: The transition to high calcium leads to a reorganization of focal adhesions and traction stresses to cells at the colony periphery, while cells in the colony interior solely engage cell-cell adhesions.
source: In our previous work, we demonstrated that this transition leads to a reorganization of focal adhesions and traction stresses to cells at the colony periphery, while cells in the colony interior solely engage cell-cell adhesions (Mertz et al., 2013; Figure 2A).
evidence: Cited from prior published work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells at the colony periphery display a biased nuclear position toward the colony center while cells within the colony interior display a central nuclear position.
source: We also documented that cells at the colony periphery display a biased nuclear position toward the colony center while cells within the colony interior display a central nuclear position (Figure 2A), suggesting that LINC complex tension might be distinct between MKCs at the colony periphery and interior (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior published work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Stretching of MKCs leads to the release of emerin from the nuclear lamina; abrogating this mechanical response also leads to precocious differentiation.
source: Indeed, stretching of MKCs leads to the release of emerin from the nuclear lamina; abrogating this mechanical response also leads to precocious differentiation (Le et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: The conformational epitope in lamin A/C examined in this work overlaps with binding sites for DNA, histones, SUN proteins, and the integral inner nuclear membrane protein emerin.
source: Interestingly, the conformational epitope in lamin A/C examined in this work (Figure 2) overlaps with binding sites for DNA, histones, SUN proteins, and the integral inner nuclear membrane protein emerin (Haque et al., 2010; Ihalainen et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: The EDC consists of 60 consecutive genes necessary for epidermal stratification and the production of the cornified envelope.
source: First, during basal stem cell differentiation, a large chromosomal region termed the epidermal differentiation complex (EDC), which consists of 60 consecutive genes necessary for epidermal stratification and the production of the cornified envelope, relocates away from the nuclear lamina toward the nuclear interior to be transcriptionally activated (Gdula et al., 2013; Mardaryev et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from prior published work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The EDC relocation during differentiation is associated with the loss of H3K27me3 chromatin marks on differentiation-specific genes.
source: The chromosome region housing the EDC moves away from the nuclear lamina during epidermal differentiation (Gdula et al., 2013; Mardaryev et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2002) and is associated with the loss of H3K27me3 chromatin marks on differentiation-specific genes (Lien et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: Most genes with annotated ATAC-seq peak(s) are conserved between WT and Sun dKO MKCs cultured in low calcium media (9307 genes).
source: Globally, most genes with annotated ATAC-seq peak(s) are conserved between WT and Sun dKO MKCs cultured in low calcium media (9307 genes, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sun dKO MKCs showed a loss of 1070 genes with annotated ATAC-seq peaks compared to WT MKCs.
source: Sun dKO MKCs showed a loss of 1070 genes with annotated ATAC-seq peaks compared to WT MKCs, which are outnumbered by gains in Sun dKO MKCs (2935 genes; Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sun dKO MKCs showed gains of 2935 genes with annotated ATAC-seq peaks compared to WT MKCs.
source: Sun dKO MKCs showed a loss of 1070 genes with annotated ATAC-seq peaks compared to WT MKCs, which are outnumbered by gains in Sun dKO MKCs (2935 genes; Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a relatively modest increase in global chromatin accessibility in Sun dKO MKCs.
source: Taken together, we conclude that there is a relatively modest increase in global chromatin accessibility in Sun dKO MKCs.
evidence: Inferred from the ATAC-seq data showing more genes gained than lost but most genes conserved.

claim: LINC complexes are required to maintain a closed, inhibited state of the EDC in undifferentiated keratinocytes.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that LINC complexes are required to maintain a closed, inhibited state of the EDC in undifferentiated keratinocytes, providing a mechanism by which loss of LINC complexes leads to precocious keratinocyte differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the ATAC-seq data showing increased accessibility at the EDC in Sun dKO cells.

claim: Tension on the nucleus through LINC complexes requires integrin engagement in undifferentiated epidermal stem cells.
source: Using a molecular biosensor, we find that tension on the nucleus through linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complexes requires integrin engagement in undifferentiated epidermal stem cells and is released during differentiation concomitant with decreased tension on A-type lamins.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements and lamin A/C antibody staining data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tension on the nucleus through LINC complexes is released during differentiation concomitant with decreased tension on A-type lamins.
source: Using a molecular biosensor, we find that tension on the nucleus through linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complexes requires integrin engagement in undifferentiated epidermal stem cells and is released during differentiation concomitant with decreased tension on A-type lamins.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in colony interior cells and lamin A/C antibody staining data in Figure 2.

claim: LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation in vivo and in vitro.
source: LINC complex ablation in mice reveals that LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation in vivo and in vitro and influence accessibility of epidermal differentiation genes, suggesting that force transduction from engaged integrins to the nucleus plays a role in maintaining keratinocyte progenitors.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of data including histology, EdU pulse-chase, RNA FISH, RT-qPCR in Sun dKO mice and cells.

claim: LINC complexes influence accessibility of epidermal differentiation genes.
source: LINC complex ablation in mice reveals that LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation in vivo and in vitro and influence accessibility of epidermal differentiation genes, suggesting that force transduction from engaged integrins to the nucleus plays a role in maintaining keratinocyte progenitors.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data showing increased accessibility at the EDC in Sun dKO cells.

claim: Force transduction from engaged integrins to the nucleus plays a role in maintaining keratinocyte progenitors.
source: LINC complex ablation in mice reveals that LINC complexes are required to repress epidermal differentiation in vivo and in vitro and influence accessibility of epidermal differentiation genes, suggesting that force transduction from engaged integrins to the nucleus plays a role in maintaining keratinocyte progenitors.
evidence: This is a suggested interpretation based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: This work reveals a direct mechanotransduction pathway capable of relaying adhesion-specific signals to regulate cell fate.
source: This work reveals a direct mechanotransduction pathway capable of relaying adhesion-specific signals to regulate cell fate.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the integration of all experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: The N2G-JM-TSMod construct is distinct from previously described Nesprin tension sensors in its design.
source: This construct is distinct from previously described Nesprin tension sensors in its design (Arsenovic et al., 2016; Déjardin et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated as a comparison to prior work with citations.

claim: Cells migrating through constrictions or plated at high versus low packing density display lower tension on a distinct Nesprin TSMod variant.
source: Of note, cells migrating through constrictions or plated at high versus low packing density display lower tension on a distinct Nesprin TSMod variant similar in design to the one described here, suggesting that tension on the LINC complex may respond to a number of mechanical inputs depending on the experimental system (Déjardin et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: High tension on the LINC complex at the edge of cell monolayer upon wounding compared to the interior of the monolayer is in line with the integrin dependence observed in this study.
source: However, high tension on the LINC complex at the edge of cell monolayer upon wounding compared to the interior of the monolayer (Déjardin et al., 2020) is in line with the integrin dependence observed in this study.
evidence: Cited from prior published work and compared to findings in this study.

claim: Sun dKO MKCs still have focal adhesions in peripheral cells despite expressing differentiation markers throughout the colony.
source: While we demonstrated that WT MKCs biased expression of differentiation markers such as Sprr1b and Ivl at the colony interior over the colony periphery (Figure 2F, G) in agreement with repressive signals from integrin engagement in cells at the colony periphery, Sun dKO MKC colonies instead expressed Sprr1b mRNAs in MKCs residing in both the interior and periphery (Figure 4E), despite still having focal adhesions in peripheral cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by paxillin immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Control over nuclear position in MKCs at the periphery of cohesive colonies is dictated by a 'tug-of-war' between the actomyosin and microtubule networks.
source: In our prior work, we found that control over nuclear position in MKCs at the periphery of cohesive colonies was dictated by a 'tug-of-war' between the actomyosin and microtubule networks (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior published work.

claim: All Nesprin TSMod constructs devised to date lack the spectrin repeats responsible for mediating interactions with microtubules and microtubule motors.
source: Whether coupling of microtubules to LINC complexes contributes to building tension on the LINC-actin-integrin axis, and the magnitude of these intramolecular forces, remains an open question as all Nesprin TSMod constructs devised to date (Arsenovic et al., 2016; Déjardin et al., 2020), including the one we describe here, lack the spectrin repeats responsible for mediating interactions with microtubules and microtubule motors (Schneider et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as a limitation of current tension sensor designs with citations to prior work.

claim: The geometry of exogenous force application to cells may influence nuclear lamina-dependent regulation of gene expression by modulating the extent of chromatin stretch.
source: Examining whether the geometry of exogenous force application to cells influences nuclear lamina-dependent regulation of gene expression by modulating the extent of chromatin stretch (Tajik et al., 2016) represents another exciting direction.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions with citation to relevant prior work.

claim: ATAC-seq data do not reveal a global shift in chromatin accessibility in the absence and presence of LINC complex engagement, as observed previously in response to critical stretch of keratinocyte monolayers.
source: We note, however, that our ATAC-seq data do not reveal a global shift in chromatin accessibility in the absence and presence of LINC complex engagement, as observed previously in response to critical stretch of keratinocyte monolayers (Le et al., 2016; Nava et al., 2020), suggesting that constitutive tension on the LINC complex and the response to rapid stretching or cyclic stretch of the cell substratum may drive distinct responses.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ATAC-seq data in this study to prior published work on mechanical stretch.

claim: Constitutive tension on the LINC complex and the response to rapid stretching or cyclic stretch of the cell substratum may drive distinct responses.
source: We note, however, that our ATAC-seq data do not reveal a global shift in chromatin accessibility in the absence and presence of LINC complex engagement, as observed previously in response to critical stretch of keratinocyte monolayers (Le et al., 2016; Nava et al., 2020), suggesting that constitutive tension on the LINC complex and the response to rapid stretching or cyclic stretch of the cell substratum may drive distinct responses.
evidence: This is a suggested interpretation based on comparison of findings to prior work.

claim: Sun dKO mice die after birth.
source: Although Sun1-/-/Sun2-/- (hereafter Sun dKO) mice die after birth (Zhang et al., 2009), we were able to analyze the developing epidermis of Sun dKO mice at E15.5.
evidence: Cited from prior published work characterizing the Sun dKO mouse model.

claim: The laminin receptors α3β1 and the hemidesmosome-specific α6β4 are the chief epidermal integrins.
source: Proliferative keratinocyte progenitor cells bind to the basement membrane via several integrin-based adhesions with the laminin receptors α3β1 and the hemidesmosome-specific α6β4 being the chief epidermal integrins (reviewed in Burgeson and Christiano, 1997).
evidence: Cited from a review article and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: MKCs lacking β1 integrin expression possess high levels of actomyosin contractility and can still engage with the substrate through β6 integrins.
source: As MKCs lacking β1 integrin expression possess high levels of actomyosin contractility and can still engage with the substrate through β6 integrins (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2012; Raghavan et al., 2003), these observations suggest that β1 integrin engagement is explicitly required for high tension on LINC complexes at the nuclear envelope in epidermal progenitor cells.
evidence: Cited from prior published work characterizing β1 integrin null cells.

claim: The formation of a perinuclear actin cage in response to stretching involves emerin release from the nuclear lamina.
source: Indeed, stretching of MKCs leads to the release of emerin from the nuclear lamina; abrogating this mechanical response also leads to precocious differentiation (Le et al., 2016). Moreover, this response involves the formation of a perinuclear actin cage, a structure that we found previously to be perturbed in MKCs lacking SUN2 (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the connection between two cited studies showing emerin release and perinuclear actin cage formation are related responses.
